name: Caribbean Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Caribbean home cooking: ackee and saltfish, jerk chicken with rice and peas, curry channa, run down mackerel, Cuban black bean soup, Haitian griot and a Saturday curry goat. Brown rice, plantain and yuca for the carbs, Scotch bonnet, thyme and allspice for the soul, and plenty of lime.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's jerk chicken, Tuesday's curry channa, Wednesday's run down mackerel, Thursday's black bean soup, Friday's griot and Saturday's curry goat each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The shrimp, snapper and breakfasts are cooked fresh.

**Fatty fish four times.** Run down mackerel on Wednesday (it comes back at Thursday's lunch) and sardines on toast on Thursday and Sunday carry your **omega-3 and B12**, and they help with **vitamin D**. Ackee and saltfish, shrimp and snapper round out the seafood.

**The Sunday before.** Soak the week's dry kidney beans and black beans in separate bowls on Saturday night (the Prep screen gives the amounts for your size). On Sunday, simmer each with a bay leaf until tender, about 1 hour, and salt at the end. They keep 4 to 5 days chilled, so freeze a tub. Brown rice cooks fresh with each dish, about 40 minutes.

**Whole-food carbs, Caribbean style.** Brown rice, whole-wheat flatbread and dumplings, yuca and plantain do the work, with beans or chickpeas most days. Plantain is boiled or baked, never fried, and coconut milk is a spoonful at a time. The warm milk with the eggs, banana milk and peanut punch carry **calcium**.

**Pickles and heat.** Pikliz, escovitch pickle, lime and Scotch bonnet brighten the rich dishes. Make the pikliz on Thursday night, and soak the salt cod on Sunday, Wednesday and Saturday nights.

name: Chinese Home Cooking (Light)
summary: A week at the Chinese home table: congee and egg pancakes for breakfast, mapo tofu, red-braised beef, steamed fish and homemade dumplings for dinner, with mixed brown rice, whole-wheat noodles and plenty of greens.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's mapo tofu, Wednesday's chicken stir-fry, Friday's red-braised beef and Saturday's dumplings each make two portions, so Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday lunches are done. The millet porridge also feeds two breakfasts.

**Rice twice.** On Sunday, simmer 2 cups of brown rice with 1 cup of pearled barley and 6 cups of water for 45 minutes, then rest it for 10. On Thursday, cook half that. Extra freezes well. Roast the snack sweet potatoes on Sunday, too.

**Fish three times.** Scallion oil salmon on Tuesday and doubanjiang mackerel on Thursday carry the **omega-3 and vitamin D**, never on back-to-back days. Steamed sea bass on Sunday adds lean protein. Walnuts blended into soy milk, on the millet porridge and with pear help the balance, too.

**Tofu, greens and soy milk.** Calcium-set tofu, soy milk, gai lan, bok choy and napa do the calcium work without dairy. Eggs, shrimp and iodized salt help with iodine, and almonds and peanuts cover vitamin E.

**Salt with care.** Soy sauce, oyster sauce and doubanjiang are strong, so each recipe measures them, and black vinegar, ginger, scallion and Sichuan pepper's numbing tingle add the punch instead. Saturday is the long day, with the dumplings, and Friday's beef is hands-off but long.

name: East African Highlands & Coast (Light)
summary: A week of East African home cooking: misir wot and shiro on injera, a slow Saturday doro wat, Kenyan githeri and sukuma wiki, a Swahili mackerel curry and Somali suqaar. Teff, millet, sorghum and dried maize carry the grains, with greens and tomato every day and legumes on six.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's misir wot, Tuesday's githeri, Thursday's shiro, Friday's suqaar and Saturday's doro wat each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Tuesday's uji covers Wednesday's breakfast too.

**Fatty fish four times.** Mackerel on Wednesday, sardines on Sunday and sardine snacks on Tuesday and Thursday give you most of the week's **omega-3 and B12**, and help with vitamin D. The mackerel and Sunday's sardines are never leftovers, and the soft sardine bones add calcium.

**Teff, millet, sorghum and maize.** Injera is teff, rich in **iron and fibre**, so check the label for 100% teff. Millet makes the uji, sorghum goes under the suqaar and dried maize goes into the githeri. Soak the maize and beans on Monday night and pressure-cook them on Tuesday; the pot covers Tuesday's dinner and Wednesday's lunch.

**Spices with purpose.** Berbere flavours the wots, and niter kibbeh adds its butter and spice in small amounts. Chicken liver in the suqaar brings **choline and iron**, and kachumbari, basbaas and lemon keep every plate bright.

**Prep ahead.** Buy injera at an Ethiopian grocery and freeze it in portions. Cook Tuesday's uji on Monday evening while the misir wot simmers, boil Thursday's ful egg on Wednesday night, and roast the kolo mix on Wednesday while the sweet potato roasts. Cook the sorghum on Thursday evening while the shiro simmers.

name: Eastern European & Georgian Table (Light)
summary: A week at an Eastern European and Georgian table: kasha with mushrooms, borscht, gołąbki, lobio and a weekend satsivi, with herring, smoked sprats and trout for the fish, plus rye bread, kefir, pickles and herbs by the handful.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's borscht, Tuesday's lobio, Wednesday's gołąbki, Thursday's chicken with kasha, Friday's pasulj and Saturday's satsivi each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. Saturday's syrniki do the same for Sunday breakfast.

**Fish four times.** Pickled herring on Monday, smoked sprats on rye on Wednesday and Friday, and baked trout on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and B12**, and the herring and trout bring most of the week's vitamin D. The walnuts in the lobio, satsivi and pkhali add plant omega-3. Fish is always fresh or opened that day, never a leftover.

**Beans, buckwheat and rye.** White and red beans turn up in the borscht, lobio and pasulj, with buckwheat, barley and rye alongside. Together they **carry** your iron, folate, magnesium and fibre, and the peppers, cabbage and pomegranate bring vitamin C to help your body use the iron.

**Calcium, choline and a little liver.** Kefir, tvorog, sulguni, poppy seeds and the soft bones in sprats bring the **calcium**. Eggs in the kasha mornings and the borscht, plus one small chicken liver pâté on Thursday, bring the choline and B12 that are hard to reach otherwise.

**Prep ahead.** Stir the buckwheat into the kefir the night before each kefir breakfast. Cook a double batch of kasha on Monday night for Tuesday's and Wednesday's breakfasts, and roll the gołąbki on Tuesday while the lobio simmers. Saturday's satsivi is the weekend project: poach the chicken first and let the sauce settle while you make the salad.

name: Gluten-free Latin Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Latin American home cooking that is gluten-free because the cuisine is: Colombian arepas and ajiaco, Peruvian quinoa soup and salmon in ají amarillo, Brazilian galinhada and moqueca, and Mexican tacos and weekend tamales. Corn, rice, quinoa, potato, cassava and plantain take turns, with lime, cilantro and chile throughout.
howItWorks:
**Gluten-free by its ingredients.** Nothing here is a substitute: corn, rice, quinoa, potato, cassava, plantain and tapioca take turns. If you have celiac disease, check that tortillas say 100% corn, and buy masarepa, masa harina and tapioca starch from a gluten-free line. Stock, chipotles in adobo, colorau and spice blends are where hidden gluten hides.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's quinoa soup, Thursday's galinhada and Saturday's tamales each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Wednesday evening's quinoa con leche covers both Thursday and Friday breakfasts.

**Fish four times.** Salmon on Tuesday and Friday, sardines in Thursday's causa and a quick sardine plate on Sunday carry your **omega-3** and **vitamin D**, and the soft sardine bones add calcium. Flaxseed in the yogurt bowls and chia in the chía fresca add a little more omega-3 through the week.

**Sunday bean pot.** Soak about 2 cups of dried black beans overnight, then simmer them with an onion and a bay leaf for about 1 hour, salting at the end. That's enough for the week. They keep 4 to 5 days, so freeze a tub. Rice keeps 3 days, so cook it close to the day.

**Eggs, dairy and greens.** Eggs carry **choline**, and so do beef, chicken and a little liver. Queijo coalho, yogurt and milk carry calcium, and kale, spinach and beans carry **iron and folate** most days.

name: Gluten-free Mediterranean (Light)
summary: A week of Mediterranean home cooking that is gluten-free by its ingredients: Greek fasolada and gemista, Spanish tortilla and lentejas, Provençal socca and pistou, and a weekend saffron risotto and polenta. Buckwheat, potatoes, rice, polenta, chickpea flour and beans take turns, with olive oil, lemon and fresh herbs throughout.
howItWorks:
**Gluten-free by its ingredients.** Buckwheat, potatoes, rice, cornmeal, chickpea flour and beans have always carried this cuisine, so most of it needs no substitute. Stock, chorizo, polenta, chickpea flour, buckwheat and spice blends can hide wheat or share a mill, so if you have celiac disease, buy sealed packs marked gluten-free.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's fasolada, Tuesday's gemista and Thursday's lentejas each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's tortilla also gives you Sunday's breakfast.

**Oily fish four times.** Salmon on Wednesday and mackerel on Friday help with **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, with canned sardines on Thursday and Sunday. Tuna in Monday's niçoise and a snack or two, plus Saturday's shrimp and mussels, add protein, iodine and zinc.

**A different starch most nights.** Beans on Monday, rice on Tuesday, potatoes on Wednesday, lentils on Thursday, chickpea flour on Friday, rice again in Saturday's risotto and polenta on Sunday. Buckwheat is at breakfast.

**Prep ahead.** Soak the cannellini for Monday's fasolada on Sunday night, and for Saturday's soupe au pistou on Thursday or Friday. Toast a jar of buckwheat for the yogurt mornings, and boil a few eggs.

name: Gluten-free South Asian (Light)
summary: A week of South Asian home cooking that is gluten-free because the cuisine is: idli and sambar, besan chilla, jowar bhakri, Kerala fish and a weekend chicken biryani. Rice, millets, dals and coconut take turns, with fish three times.
howItWorks:

name: Gulf Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Gulf home cooking: chicken machboos, lamb saloona, beef and okra marag, grilled kanaad with dakkous, roasted sardines and a slow Saturday lamb harees. Brown basmati, whole-wheat khubz and legumes, with dates, laban and nuts for snacks.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's machboos, Wednesday's saloona, Thursday's marag and Saturday's harees each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Pack the rice or bread with it.

**Fish twice, plus shrimp.** Kanaad with dakkous on Tuesday and fresh sardines on Friday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. Both are cooked fresh, three days apart, and shrimp rounds out Sunday.

**Whole grains the Gulf way.** Brown basmati in the machboos, marag and shrimp, whole-wheat khubz, and cracked wheat in the harees. Dates are a small sweetness, one or two at a time, so the **glycaemic load** stays in check.

**Breakfasts that rotate.** Foul, balaleet-inspired vermicelli and tomato eggs each come round two or three times, never on back-to-back mornings. The eggs and fava beans carry your **choline and a good share of your iron**, and laban or milk snacks keep **calcium** up.

**Weekend project.** Saturday's harees is mostly hands-off simmering. Cooking fats are the Gulf kitchen's own, vegetable oil and a little ghee, with olive oil for salads and the nakhi.

name: Filipino, Malaysian & Indonesian Table (Light)
summary: A week of Filipino, Malaysian and Indonesian home cooking: bubur ayam, nasi lemak and tapsilog breakfasts, chicken adobo, mackerel sinigang, pinakbet, a lighter beef rendang, gado-gado, a laksa-inspired weekend soup and grilled mackerel with sambal, all on brown rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Tuesday's adobo, Wednesday's tempeh stir-fry, Thursday's pinakbet, Friday's rendang and Saturday's laksa each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The kacang hijau makes two bowls too. The mackerel is always cooked fresh.

**Rice batch.** On Sunday, cook 1½ cups of dry brown rice (about 4½ cups cooked) for Monday to Wednesday, and simmer Monday's bubur base while you're at it. On Wednesday night, cook another 1½ cups dry (about 4½ cups cooked) for Thursday to Sunday. It keeps 4 or 5 days in the fridge. Press a little into a block on Sunday for Monday's gado-gado.

**Fish four times.** Mackerel sinigang on Monday, sardine sambal on Wednesday and Friday and mackerel ikan bakar on Sunday bring your **omega-3**, and the sardine bones bring calcium. None of them land on back-to-back days.

**Coconut as flavour.** Coconut milk goes in by the spoonful, for the nasi lemak rice, the rendang, the laksa and the kacang hijau. The cooking oil is canola, in small amounts, so **saturated fat stays under 10%**.

**Salt, and a little liver.** Soy sauce, fish sauce and shrimp paste do most of the salting, plus a measured pinch of salt, and each recipe measures them. A little chicken liver in the bubur ayam, as many Jakarta cooks do, brings **vitamin A, B12 and choline**.

name: Japanese & Korean Home Table (Light)
summary: A week at the Japanese and Korean home table: miso soup, grilled fish, soba, rice bowls, namul and a hot pot, with brown rice and barley, tofu and plenty of vegetables.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's teriyaki, Wednesday's jjigae and Saturday's bibimbap each make two portions, so Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday lunches are done. The banchan and the dak-juk are also made once for two breakfasts.

**Sunday prep.** Cook a big pot of brown rice and pearl barley, portion it, and cook a second batch on Wednesday night. It keeps four days, so every rice meal is a quick reheat. Roast a tray of sweet potatoes and make a jar of nut jorim too.

**Fish three times.** Salmon on Tuesday, mackerel on Thursday and a quick salmon soba on Saturday bring your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, never two days in a row. Walnuts in the snacks and the porridge add more.

**Soy, seaweed and noodles.** Tofu, natto, edamame and the bean pastes carry protein, and calcium-set tofu carries calcium. Nori and wakame add iodine. Soba and udon take turns with the rice so the week never turns into a rice wall.

**Saturday is the long day.** Dak-juk in the morning and bibimbap at night take the most time, so weeknights stay quick. Miso, tamari and kimchi bring the salt, so each recipe measures them and lets ginger, vinegar and mandarin add the brightness.

name: Keto Asian (Light)
summary: A week of grilled fish, stir-fries, a green curry, a Korean lettuce-wrap spread and a hot pot, with no rice, noodles or sugar. Net carbs stay at 40 g or less every day, and the fat comes from fish, avocado, nuts, sesame and a little coconut.
howItWorks:
**Where the carbs went.** There is no rice, noodle or sugar here. Cauliflower rice stands in once, lettuce wraps the beef, and with no sugar the flavour comes from garlic, chili, sesame and fermented pastes. Greens, mushrooms and tofu fill the plate, so net carbs stay under the keto ceiling every day.

**Fat from fish, nuts and avocado.** Salmon, mackerel, avocado, walnuts, pumpkin seeds and sesame carry the calories. Canola does the frying, with perilla or sesame oil to finish. Coconut is light and shows up only in the green curry and the tom yum, so saturated fat stays under 10%.

**Fatty fish three times.** Salmon on Tuesday and Saturday mornings and mackerel on Thursday night bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, never on back-to-back days. Sea bass in Friday's tom yum and Sunday's hot pot is the lean fish. Perilla oil, walnuts and fish carry the omega-3 that balances the sesame.

**Greens carry the vitamins.** Spinach, bok choy, gai lan or lettuce is at nearly every meal for **folate, vitamin C, vitamin K and potassium**. Calcium-set tofu, gai lan and bok choy do the calcium work without dairy, pumpkin seeds add magnesium, pork brings thiamin, and a few clams in Monday's stew add a big hit of B12.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The curry, mapo tofu, ginger chicken, bulgogi wraps and krapow each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Sunday's hot pot is a one-pot finish. Doubanjiang, gochujang and doenjang usually contain wheat, so anyone avoiding gluten should look for gluten-free versions, and check the miso and kimchi labels too.

name: Keto Mediterranean (Light)
summary: A week of Greek, Italian and Spanish food that happens to be very low in carbs: roast trout and sardines, souvlaki, a weekend moussaka, big salads and plenty of olive oil, olives, avocado and nuts. Net carbs stay at 40 g or less every day, with leafy greens and vegetables doing the vitamin work.
howItWorks:
**Fat from the Mediterranean pantry.** Most of the fat comes from olive oil, olives, avocado, hazelnuts, almonds, walnuts and chia, with trout, sardines and shrimp for the protein. Butter, cream and bacon never appear. There is no cheese, and Greek yogurt is the only dairy, so saturated fat stays low.

**Where the carbs went.** There are no grains, potatoes, sugar or beans here. Fruit is a few raspberries, lemon and avocado, and onion, tomato and garlic are measured like seasoning. Every day stays under the keto ceiling for net carbs, whatever size you eat.

**Vegetables carry the vitamins.** Leafy greens fill every day, with rapini, zucchini, mushrooms and eggplant on the days they suit. They bring **folate, vitamin A, potassium and calcium**, and chia, hazelnuts and sardines with their soft bones help with magnesium and calcium.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's souvlaki, Wednesday's pork, Friday's cacciatore and Saturday's moussaka each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. **Fish** lands on Tuesday, Friday and Sunday, always cooked or opened fresh.

**Sunday prep.** Make one jar of chia pudding for Monday, and three more on Thursday night for Friday to Sunday. Cube and marinate the souvlaki pork on Monday morning, so dinner is quick.

summary: A week at a Levantine table. Foul, labneh and balila for breakfast, lentils, chickpeas and bulgur on most days, lamb and chicken in moderation, and fish three times. Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian and Jordanian dishes, with sumac, za'atar, tahini and plenty of herbs.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's shish tawook, Tuesday's mujadara, Thursday's adas bi hamod and Saturday's kibbeh each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's ijjeh does the same for Sunday breakfast.

**Fish three times.** Salmon samke harra on Wednesday, sardines on Friday and mackerel on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. They are never back to back, and always cooked fresh.

**Legumes most days.** Fava beans, chickpeas and lentils turn up at breakfast, lunch or dinner. With bulgur and whole-wheat pita they cover your **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon and tomato beside them help your body use the iron.

**Prep ahead.** The Sunday before, boil a few eggs for the week's breakfasts. On Thursday evening, while the soup simmers, make a batch of hummus for the Friday and Sunday snacks. Saturday's kibbeh is the weekend project, so soak the bulgur first and get the oven hot.

name: Diabetes-friendly Mediterranean (Light)
summary: Diabetes-friendly home cooking from Greece, southern Italy, Spain and Crete: beans, lentils and chickpeas every day, big salads first, small portions of barley, farro, pasta and rye, and fresh or canned fish most days.
howItWorks:
**Steady carbs, three times a day.** Breakfast, lunch and dinner each get a small, honest portion of starch: a thin slice of rye, a few spoonfuls of barley or farro, a handful of whole-wheat pasta. It always sits next to beans, lentils, eggs, fish or chicken, so the starch digests more slowly.

**Legumes at most meals.** Lentils, chickpeas, white beans and lupini turn up at two meals on most days and carry the **fibre and protein**. Pasta e ceci has far more chickpea than pasta, and the orzotto is mostly chicken, mushrooms, broccoli and beans.

**Salad and vegetables first.** Arugula, tomato, cucumber and big trays of vegetables come with the meal, with lemon, red wine or sherry vinegar for the sour. Eat the crunch first and the starch last.

**Fish most days.** Sardines on Tuesday, salmon on Friday and mackerel on Sunday bring **omega-3**, cooked the day they are bought or thawed. Canned mussels and sardines on rye add B12 and iron on other days, and the soft sardine bones bring calcium.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Orzotto, souvlaki, lentejas, fasolada and the frittata each make two portions, so the next meal is already done. On Sunday, simmer the lentils for Monday's salad, and grate the tomato for the tostadas the night before. Soak the beans on Friday night for Saturday's fasolada.

name: Diabetes-friendly South Asian (Light)
summary: Diabetes-friendly home cooking from Punjab, Gujarat, Kerala, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, built around dal, beans and vegetables, with small portions of roti, brown basmati, millet and barley. Steady carbs, plenty of fibre, fish twice and a weekend barley haleem.
howItWorks:
**Steady carbs, three times a day.** Each meal gets one modest portion of starch: one roti, a spoonful or two of brown basmati, or a little millet or barley. On the Light size these are small, a palm-sized roti or a spoonful of rice, and dal and vegetables fill the plate. It always comes with dal, beans, yogurt, fish or chicken, so the starch digests more slowly.

**Big dal, small rice, salad first.** Moong, toor, chana dal, rajma and chickpeas turn up at two meals on most days and carry **fibre and protein**. Kachumber, raita, thoran and mallung come with the meal, with lemon or tamarind for the sour. Eat the crunch first and the starch last.

**Fish on Tuesday and Friday.** Kerala-style mackerel curry and Sri Lankan pepper and tamarind salmon bring **omega-3** and vitamin D, and both are cooked fresh. Rajma, tuvar dal, the tandoori tray and Saturday's haleem each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done.

**Sunday prep.** Cook a pot of brown basmati for the first rice dinners and freeze a portion for Friday. Boil the week's eggs too. Soak the chana dal and millet on Wednesday and Saturday nights for the upma mornings, and the moong dal for each chilla morning.

**Eggs, curd and milk.** A boiled egg or an egg chaat turns up as a street snack on a few days and adds **choline and protein**. Curd, haldi doodh and paneer cover calcium and B12. Canola does the cooking, with just a spoonful of ghee on the dals and the haleem.

name: North African Spice Road (Light)
summary: A week on the North African spice road. Chakchouka, bissara and msemen for breakfast, a chicken and apricot tagine, harira, chermoula sardines, Algerian couscous and a slow lamb and prune tagine, with ras el hanout, harissa, preserved lemon and saffron throughout.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chicken tagine, Tuesday's harira, Thursday's couscous and Saturday's lamb and prune tagine each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Tuesday evening's bissara pot also covers Wednesday and Thursday breakfasts. Pack the khobz or couscous separately.

**Fish most days.** Fresh sardines on Wednesday and harissa mackerel on Friday are the two fish dinners. Tinned mackerel, a sardine sandwich, sardine kefta and a tuna slata mechouia turn up at lunch and snack time, as they do in Moroccan and Tunisian kitchens, for **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**.

**Legumes most days.** Fava in the bissara, lentils in the harira, and chickpeas in the tagines, couscous and snacks carry your **iron, folate and fibre**. The lemon, tomato and preserved lemon beside them help your body use the iron.

**Olive oil, whole grains and nuts.** Olive oil is the only cooking fat. Whole-wheat khobz and couscous replace the white ones, with oats and barley alongside. Almonds go in the tagines, and walnuts go with the dates.

**Prep ahead.** The Sunday before, toast a jar of almonds and walnuts for the porridge. Cook the bissara on Tuesday while the harira simmers, and make Saturday's zaalouk on Friday night. Saturday's lamb tagine is the slow project, and the msemen is the slow breakfast.

summary: A week of Egyptian and Sudanese home cooking: ful, ta'meya and shakshuka for breakfast, molokhia, koshari and bamia from Cairo, grilled sardines and sayadeya from Alexandria, and a peanut mullah from Sudan. Tahini, lemon and fresh salad keep every plate bright.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's molokhia, Tuesday's koshari, Thursday's bamia and Friday's mullah each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's sayadeya and ta'meya cover Sunday.

**Fish every day.** A sardine sandwich on Monday, ful with sardines on Tuesday, grilled sardines on Wednesday, mackerel in tomato on Thursday, a sardine snack on Friday and Saturday's sayadeya (reheated on Sunday) carry your **omega-3**. Tahini, peanuts and sesame lean omega-6, and the fish keeps the balance honest.

**Legumes most days.** Fava, lentils, chickpeas and lupini turn up at breakfast, lunch, dinner or snack time for **iron, folate and fibre**. The lemon, tomato and parsley beside them help your body use the iron.

**Vitamins A and E.** Molokhia, spinach, carrots and sweet potato carry **vitamin A**, and a spoonful of dukkah, almonds or peanuts most days carries vitamin E. Sunday's chicken liver adds B12 and iron.

**Prep ahead.** On Friday night soak the dried fava for Saturday's ta'meya. On Sunday, cook the lentil and rice base for Tuesday's koshari. The Prep screen gives the exact amounts for your size. Brown Saturday's onions the day before.

name: Nordic Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Nordic home cooking: porridge and skyr for breakfast, rye with herring or egg and shrimp, Swedish meatballs, Finnish salmon soup, Swedish pea soup, Norwegian lapskaus and a gravlax-style salmon supper. Rye, barley, oats, potatoes and root vegetables carry the starch, with berries, dill and pickles for brightness.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's meatballs, Tuesday's lapskaus, Wednesday's salmon soup, Thursday's pea soup and Saturday's chicken soup each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Put the yellow peas to soak on Wednesday night.

**Fatty fish four times.** Pickled herring on Monday, salmon soup on Wednesday and again for Thursday's lunch, and a gravlax-style salmon supper on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. On other days, vitamin D mushrooms on crispbread and an egg most days help.

**Rye, barley and oats.** Porridge, skyr with toasted oats, dark rye, crispbread and pearl barley carry the grains, with potatoes and root vegetables alongside. Rapeseed (canola) oil is the everyday fat, with a little butter, and hazelnuts add **vitamin E and magnesium**.

**Four countries, plus Iceland.** Sweden brings the meatballs, pea soup and pytt i panna, Finland the salmon soup, Norway the lapskaus, and Denmark the open-faced rye, fishcakes and chicken soup. Icelandic skyr is the breakfast. Dill, pickled beets, horseradish and lingonberry keep the plates bright.

**Weekend project.** Start the gravlax on Saturday morning: rub it, wrap it, weigh it down and leave it in the fridge. By Sunday supper it is silky, and the dill potatoes take 20 minutes. Saturday's chicken soup is the other slow pot.

summary: A week of North American comfort food made bright: steel-cut oats and egg muffins for breakfast, a bison burger, turkey chili, Québec split pea soup, a Minnesota wild rice hotdish, a blackened Cobb and two kinds of salmon. Familiar, filling and full of vegetables, beans and fish.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's sheet-pan chicken, Tuesday's turkey chili, Wednesday's hotdish, Thursday's split pea soup and Saturday's baked beans each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The egg muffins cover two breakfasts. The burger, the Cobb and both salmon dinners are cooked fresh.

**Fish twice.** Maritime salmon cakes on Friday and a maple-mustard salmon on Sunday carry your **omega-3** and help with **vitamin D**. They never land back to back, and both are served fresh. The canned salmon's soft bones add calcium.

**Batch your breakfasts.** Bake a tin of egg muffins on Sunday for Monday and Tuesday. Cook a pot of steel-cut oats on Tuesday night for Wednesday, Friday and Saturday. Reheat the oats with a splash of milk, and the muffins in the microwave for 45 seconds.

**Beans and greens.** Kidney beans in the chili, split peas on Thursday and white beans on Saturday give you **iron, folate and fibre**, with kale and spinach stirred into the pots. Bison, turkey and chicken take turns, and cider vinegar, pickled onion, apple and cranberry keep every plate bright.

**Prep ahead.** On Sunday, bake the muffins, shred the cabbage for Monday's slaw and pickle the onion. Rinse and soak the wild rice on Wednesday morning, and sear the chicken and boil the egg for Saturday's Cobb on Friday night.

summary: A week of Punjabi, Delhi, Lahori and Lucknowi home cooking: dal palak, rajma, chicken karahi, saag paneer, a mackerel curry and a Saturday nihari-inspired goat stew, with oily fish twice and whole-wheat roti and brown basmati in place of naan and white rice.
howItWorks:

**Fish on Friday and Sunday.** Atlantic mackerel curry and tandoori-spiced salmon bring your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. Both are cooked fresh, never reheated, and they sit two days apart.

**Eggs, legumes and dahi.** An egg starts every morning, from one boiled egg in the daliya to anda chilla and bhurji, and it carries your **choline**. Dal, rajma and chickpeas turn up on most days, and dahi, lassi and haldi doodh keep calcium up.

**Ghee in small amounts.** Everyday cooking uses canola oil. Ghee finishes the dal, khichdi and saag tadkas and brushes the paratha, which keeps saturated fat low. Brown basmati appears on four days, and roti on the rest.

**Weekend prep.** Cook the chicken for Monday's chaat and make Monday's daliya on Sunday night, knead atta dough the night before a bhurji morning, and save Saturday afternoon for the nihari, which is mostly hands-off simmering.

name: Persian & Turkish Table (Light)
summary: A week at a Persian and Turkish table. Menemen, nan-o-panir-o-sabzi and kuku for breakfast, then ghormeh sabzi, köfte, kuru fasulye and a weekend fesenjan with brown basmati and bulgur, herbs by the handful, and fish three times.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's ghormeh sabzi, Tuesday's köfte, Thursday's kuru fasulye and Saturday's fesenjan each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. Saturday's kuku sabzi does the same for Sunday breakfast.

**Rice and beans in batches.** Cook enough brown basmati for two portions on Monday and again on Saturday, steamed under a tea towel. Soak Thursday's white beans on Wednesday night. Both keep 4 to 5 days in the fridge.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Wednesday, salmon on Friday and mackerel on Sunday carry your **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**. They are never back to back, and always cooked fresh. Walnuts in the nan-o-panir and the fesenjan add plant omega-3 on the other days.

**Herbs, greens and calcium.** Parsley, cilantro, dill, mint and scallion fill the ghormeh sabzi, kuku and herb rice, with kale and arugula alongside, for **vitamin K, folate and iron**. Feta, yogurt, tahini and kale bring the calcium.

**Prep ahead.** Boil the egg for each nan-o-panir morning the night before, and soak the beans on Wednesday night. Saturday's fesenjan is the slow weekend project, so start it mid-afternoon and let it bubble while you finish dinner.

howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's feijoada, Wednesday's lentil guiso, Friday's lomo saltado and Saturday's moqueca each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The salmon, sardines and ajiaco are cooked fresh.

**Fatty fish four times.** Salmon with pebre on Tuesday, sardines with yuca on Thursday and mackerel moqueca on Saturday (back for Sunday lunch) carry your **omega-3** and help with **vitamin D**. Sardine bones add calcium, and Monday's cod ceviche brings iodine.

name: South Indian & Sri Lankan Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Tamil, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra and Sri Lankan home cooking: sambar, a sardine curry, a mackerel ambul thiyal, a Chettinad pepper chicken and a fish moilee, with red rice, brown rice and millet in place of white rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's sambar, Wednesday's Sri Lankan dhal, Friday's bisi bele bath and Saturday's Chettinad chicken each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. The fish dinners are always cooked fresh.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Tuesday, mackerel on Thursday and a Spanish mackerel moilee on Sunday carry your **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**. They never fall on back-to-back days.

**Coconut as a flavour.** Fresh coconut goes into sambols and thorans by the spoonful, with a little coconut milk in the dhal and the moilee. Frying is mostly canola, with coconut oil in the Kerala fry-ups, ghee in the bisi bele bath and gingelly oil in the ambul thiyal. That keeps **saturated fat under 10%**.

**Eggs, dal and curd.** Eggs start four mornings, and a boiled egg snack covers the pesarattu days. Dal, chickpeas, prawns, chicken or fish anchor every lunch and dinner, with red rice, brown rice and foxtail millet in place of white rice. Curd and buttermilk bring calcium, and almonds bring **vitamin E**.

**Soak ahead.** Soak the moong for the pesarattu the night before. For the hoppers, soak the rice in the morning, blend it that night and leave the batter to ferment. Cook a big batch of red rice on Sunday to save time midweek.

name: Southern African Braai & Pot (Light)
summary: A week of Southern African home cooking: bobotie with lentils, a Cape mackerel curry, Zimbabwean beef and greens with sadza, chakalaka and beans, umngqusho and a Saturday peri-peri chicken. Maize, sorghum, beans and greens carry the week, with fatty fish on five days.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's bobotie, Tuesday's fish curry, Wednesday's beef and greens, Thursday's chakalaka and beans, Friday's umngqusho and Saturday's peri-peri chicken each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. The mabele pot covers two breakfasts.

**Fatty fish on five days.** Pilchards on Monday, Tuesday's mackerel curry and Wednesday's leftover, pilchards on toast on Friday and Sunday's braaied mackerel give you most of the week's omega-3 and B12, and help with vitamin D. The soft pilchard bones add calcium. The braai is always cooked fresh.

**Maize, sorghum and beans.** Pap and sadza use whole-grain mealie meal, in modest portions. Whole sorghum makes the mabele, hominy stands in for samp, pinto beans for sugar beans, and lentils fill in the rest. Legumes turn up on most days.

**Greens and chicken livers.** Collards stand in for rape greens in the stew, umngqusho and braai greens, and chakalaka and fresh sambals keep every plate bright. The chicken livers on Saturday's peri-peri tray bring **iron, folate and choline**.

**Prep ahead.** Soak the sorghum on Monday night and cook the mabele on Tuesday evening while the curry simmers. Cook the chakalaka for Tuesday's eggs while Monday's bobotie bakes, and Saturday's while the umngqusho simmers. Soak the samp on Thursday night.

name: Thai & Vietnamese Fresh Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Thai and Vietnamese home cooking: jok, Thai omelettes and xôi for breakfast, red curry, larb, caramel mackerel, lemongrass pork and a slow phở for dinner, with fresh herbs, lime and chili everywhere and mostly brown rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Tuesday's larb, Wednesday's lemongrass pork, Thursday's red curry and Saturday's phở each make two portions, so Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday lunches are done. Saturday's xôi makes two breakfasts too, and the chè makes two bowls.

**Rice batch.** The Sunday before, cook 2 cups of dry brown rice (about 6 cups cooked) for Monday to Wednesday, then 1¾ cups on Wednesday night for Thursday to Sunday. It keeps 4 or 5 days in the fridge and freezes well, and a modest scoop goes into most meals. Rice noodles show up only in the phở and the gỏi cuốn, and rice paper only in the rolls.

**Fish three times.** Steamed salmon on Monday, grilled mackerel on Friday and mackerel kho on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and never fall on back-to-back days. Eggs and dried shrimp add choline and iodine.

**Fish sauce, measured.** Fish sauce, dried shrimp, shrimp paste and a little iodized salt are the salt here, so each recipe uses a set amount, and lime, chili, ginger, lemongrass and herbs by the handful carry the rest of the flavour.

**Calcium without dairy.** Calcium-set tofu, gai lan, water spinach, dried shrimp and fortified soy milk do the work.

name: Vegan East Asian (Light)
summary: A fully plant-based week of Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese home cooking: mapo tofu, sundubu jjigae, bibimbap, a creamy soy milk hot pot and soy milk congee. Tofu, tempeh, natto, edamame, seitan and soya chunks carry the protein, and fortified soy milk every day carries the B12.
howItWorks:
**Soy, in many forms.** Soy carries this week the way it does in Buddhist and Taiwanese vegetarian kitchens: soft and firm tofu, tempeh, natto, edamame, soya chunks and soy milk, with mung beans and seitan for a change. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day reaches at least a fifth of its calories from protein.

**B12 is fortified on purpose.** Plants don't make vitamin B12, so every day has a glass or more of **fortified soy milk**. The numbers assume about 2 µg of B12 per cup, a common US level. Many Canadian cartons carry about half that, so a daily B12 supplement is the safe bet for most vegans.

**Calcium, iron and the hard ones.** Calcium-set tofu, fortified soy milk, almonds, sesame and bok choy carry the calcium. Natto, tofu, tempeh, soya chunks and mung beans carry the iron, with vitamin C from broccoli, napa and mandarins alongside. Use iodized salt.

**Omega-3 from plants.** Ground flax goes into the congee and the warm soy milk drinks, and canola oil does most of the cooking, which keeps the omega balance in range. Sesame oil is the finishing flavour, and it also fries the kimchi for the jjigae.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The mapo tofu, bún chay, jjigae, tempeh, teriyaki and bibimbap each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's congee makes Sunday's breakfast too. On Sunday, cook about 2½ cups of dry brown rice for the week, keep it in the fridge for 4 or 5 days and freeze the rest in portions.

name: Vegan Indian (Light)
summary: A fully plant-based week of North and South Indian home cooking, from Punjabi rajma and Gujarati kadhi to Kerala tofu roast and Tamil idli. Dals, beans, tofu and soya carry the protein, and a daily mug of fortified soy beverage, in chai, haldi doodh, lassi or kheer, carries the B12.
howItWorks:
**Protein from dals, beans and soy.** Moong, toor and urad dal, rajma, chickpeas, besan, calcium-set tofu, soya chunks, soy granules and peanuts take turns, so no single food carries the week. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day reaches at least a fifth of its calories from protein.

**B12 is fortified on purpose.** Plants don't make vitamin B12, so every day has a mug or glass of **fortified soy beverage**: in the chai, haldi doodh, lassi or kheer. The numbers assume about 2 µg of B12 per cup, a common US level. Many Canadian cartons carry about half that, so a daily B12 supplement is the safe bet for most vegans.

**Calcium, iron and the hard ones.** Calcium-set tofu, fortified soy beverage and soy yogurt carry the calcium. Rajma, dals, chickpeas and tofu carry the iron, with tomato, lemon and cilantro alongside to help you absorb it. Use iodized salt, and the soy beverage adds a little **vitamin D**.

**Omega-3 from plants.** Ground flax and walnuts turn up in only a few places: the mint chutney with the chilla, the idli podi (alsi chutney powder is a real thing) and the walnuts on the fruit chaat and, at the bigger size, a til-alsi laddoo. Canola oil handles the cooking, which keeps the omega balance in range.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's rajma, Tuesday's palak tofu, Wednesday's kadhi khichdi, Thursday's keema, Friday's Kerala roast and Saturday's biryani each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Soak the rajma and the moong dal on Sunday night (and the moong again on Tuesday and Thursday nights, or blend two days of chilla batter at once) and start the idli batter on Friday afternoon.

name: West African Pot (Light)
summary: A week of West African home cooking: egusi with smoked fish, groundnut stew, red-red, chicken yassa and a Saturday fish and rice pot, built on millet, yam, sweet potato, plantain and black-eyed peas. Real palm oil for flavour, greens and groundnuts most days, and snacks you would find at a roadside stall.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's egusi, Tuesday's yassa, Wednesday's groundnut stew, Friday's red-red and Saturday's fish and rice each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Sunday's moi moi covers two breakfasts, and Friday's koko covers Saturday's.

**Oily fish.** Smoked mackerel goes into Monday's egusi, and canned sardines with their soft bones sit on warm yam on Friday and Sunday. They carry your omega-3, B12 and **vitamin D**. Thursday's tilapia is grilled fresh, and Saturday's haddock is seared fresh on both days.

**Palm oil with a purpose.** Red palm oil gives the egusi, moi moi and red-red their colour and flavour, and a lighter vegetable oil does the rest. Groundnuts (peanuts) and melon seeds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**; sardine bones, yogurt, sesame and collards keep your **calcium** up.

**Whole-food starches.** Millet, yam, sweet potato, plantain and black-eyed peas do the work, with a little brown rice in Saturday's thieb. No African grocery nearby? Mustard greens, canned or smoked fish and a hot red chili cover most of what it sells.

**Prep ahead.** Soak peas on Saturday night for Sunday's moi moi, and cook a pot for Monday's salad. On Thursday, soak millet and peas and cook the koko that evening. Make the egg sauce base on Sunday and Wednesday.
